title: GPU pool slotting, capacity models, and ops checklist (2026-Q1)
summary: Working model for how we convert GPU demand forecasts into an on-prem rack slotting plan. Includes power/thermal assumptions, per-region distribution, spare strategy, and an operational checklist for staging and live swap operations.
body:
Purpose:
This is a working capacity planning sheet and ops checklist for on-prem / colocation GPU pools. It covers how we translate forecasted vGPU-hours and target utilization into physical rack slots, power budgets, cooling margins, and an operational runbook for installs and swaps. Intended audience: infra planners, SRE, site ops, and solutions engineering.
body_continued:
Assumptions (baseline):
- Target average utilization (service-level): 60% sustained across the pool; pegged to 80% burst headroom for peak windows.
- Typical GPU node: dual-socket host with 8x L40s (or similar) per 42U rack; power per GPU (steady-state token-serving workload): 320W average, 650W peak.
- Host overhead (CPUs, NVMe, fans, BMC): 700W per host.
- Rack PDU capacity (deploy baseline): 20kW usable per rack (after distribution losses), with target fill 75% to allow redundancy and cooling margin.
- Power feed redundancy required N+1 at the pod level for production pools.
- Cold-aisle containment in all target colo sites (assumption to validate per site).
- Ambient inlet temperature target: 20-24C. Avoid >26C for high-density racks.
- Cables: max recommended power cable length from PDU to node: 1.5m; network uplink length recommendations documented in linked_artifacts.

Model steps (how to use):
1) Input forecasted GPU-hours per region (monthly): we convert to required concurrent GPU count by dividing by target utilization and average hours. Example: if forecast is 100k GPU-hours/month and we assume 720 hours/month and 60% avg util => concurrent GPUs = (100k / 720) / 0.6 ~= 232 GPUs.
2) Map concurrent GPUs to node count (GPUs per host) and racks (hosts per rack). Example: 8 GPUs/host => 29 hosts => 3 racks (assuming 12 hosts/rack depending on chassis).
3) Calculate power draw: avg GPU power * GPUs + host overhead * hosts. Compare to rack PDU usable kW and ensure <= 75% fill.
4) Add cooling headroom: target 20% additional cooling capacity per rack for thermal spikes and inlet temp variance.
5) Reserve spare capacity: +10% spare racks for hot-swap and failure handling in production pods; +1 hot spare full rack per pod for immediate swaps.

Sample quick calc (illustrative):
- Forecast region A: 150k GPU-hours/month
- Concurrent GPUs = (150000 / 720) / 0.6 = 347 GPUs => with 8 GPUs/node -> 44 hosts -> if 10 hosts/rack => 5 racks (44 hosts -> 5 racks; last rack partially filled).
- Power: GPUs avg 320W * 347 = 111kW; hosts overhead 700W * 44 = 30.8kW => total ~142kW across 5 racks => ~28.4kW per rack -> exceeds our baseline PDU usable 20kW. Options: reduce hosts/rack density (spread across more racks), request higher PDU capacity (30kW+), or use lower-power GPUs/limits.

Slotting heuristics (practical rules we use):
- Keep max 70% of PDU usable kW as steady-state target.
- Prefer odd-even rack slotting for airflow: distribute high-draw hosts across racks to avoid thermal hotspots.
- Group similar model/quantization variants together for cache locality (where possible) but prioritize power balance over model locality.
- Reserve the top 4U of each rack for PDUs, switches, and sensor nodes (per colo standard).

Operational checklist (before rack install):
- Validate site power capacity and feed redundancy with colo tech ops (PDU types, breaker ratings, A/B path).
- Confirm cold-aisle containment and CRAC setpoints. If site lacks containment, plan +25% cooling margin.
- Order PDUs with appropriate outlet density and remote metering (SNMP) – prefer switched PDUs for granular power cycling.
- Label all racks with unique pod/rack IDs and mount thermal sensors at 1/3 and 2/3 height.
- Stage hosts in our staging lab for burn-in tests (48 hours at 80% power draw).
- Prepare spare inventory: 1 spare GPU per 12 deployed GPUs, 1 spare host per 36 hosts, spare PSU rails/cables per rack.

Live-swap / replacement runbook (high level):
1) Page on-call site ops and SRE who owns the pod.
2) Shift load away from target host (reroute requests or use canary diversion) if possible.
3) Power-cycle via PDU remote outlet; if unresponsive, coordinate physical pull.
4) Pull failed host to warm staging rack in colo, replace with pre-staged spare host; reattach to network, restore node config via PXE/ansible.
5) Update inventory sheet and incident record (link to JIRA ticket).

Unresolved questions / decisions needed:
- Minimum acceptable PDU usable kW per rack for L40-class decks in our current pod design (today we assume 20kW but this may be insufficient). Decision by infra leads.
- Strategy for mixing lower-power quantized model racks with full-power racks: allow mixed racks or fully separate? Impacts cost and density.
- Policy for cold spare racks vs. distributed spare hosts. Tradeoff between switchover time and unused capital.

Open TODOs:
- Run per-site audit to confirm cold-aisle presence and exact CRAC capabilities (owner: Arielle). Due: 2025-12-01.
- Update pod design templates with 30kW-rated PDU options and compare colo pricing (owner: Marcus). Due: 2026-01-20.
- Simulate failure scenarios with gpu-pod-simulator for 10k random host failures to validate spare strategy (owner: Diego). Due: 2026-02-05.

Appendix (quick references):
- Useful conversion: 1 GPU-hour @ 320W -> 0.32 kWh.
- Emergency contacts: colo NOC, cross-connect rep, power engineer (see internal contacts).
- Related docs: see linked_artifacts above for JIRA/confluence references.

Notes to self (informal):
- Avoid over-optimizing for 8x chassis; some sites prefer 4x high-power nodes which changes rack math. Keep models flexible.
- Cable management becomes a major time sink for dense racks: pre-stage harnesses and color-code.
- When in doubt for production pods, prefer extra cooling headroom over higher density.

Document history: draft created 2025-11-15 by Marcus, iterative updates by Arielle and Diego through Jan 2026.
